paras: The threatened lynching of Jed Pritchett followed a June 1888 accusation that Pritchett, a Black man, had assaulted an eight-year-old white girl near Danville in Pittsylvania County, Virginia. Armed men and officers searched for him while Virginia papers predicted, and in some cases openly hoped, that he would be lynched when caught. He was arrested in North Carolina in December, and the sheriff moved him to Lynchburg for fear of an attack on the jail.
Pritchett, described as about 30 and formerly of Caswell County, North Carolina, had once worked for W. C. Pollok, a farmer on Sandy Creek some eight or nine miles from Danville.

According to the Danville Register, Pollok's daughter Jennie went to a spring about 150 yards from the house on Sunday afternoon, June 24, to fetch water for her grandfather. Half an hour later she reached the house and named Pritchett, who was lying near the spring, as her attacker. Her father was away, and her grandfather took a double-barrel shotgun and went after Pritchett, who had fled. Her life was at first despaired of, but by the end of the week she was reported out of danger.

On June 25 a party was organized at Danville to hunt for him, and the Alexandria Gazette reported that "a number of determined men" were scouring the country. The Register said officers and friends of the Pollok family were searching and that Pritchett was supposed to have gone toward Milton in Caswell County.

Through the summer Pritchett was several times reported caught, and on August 10 a Danville correspondent wrote that he was "positively asserted" to be in jail at Roxboro, North Carolina. In late December the Danville police arrested him near Durham, North Carolina, and took him to the Pittsylvania County jail at Chatham. Fearing an attack by lynchers, the sheriff then removed him to the Lynchburg jail. No report of a trial or of his later fate was found.

Only white papers covered the case, beginning with a Danville telegram in the Richmond Dispatch and a Virginia News brief in the Alexandria Gazette on June 26. The Dispatch called Pritchett "a negro brute" and "the fiend" and said that if caught he would "meet with the fate he deserves," while the Gazette said he "will certainly be lynched when caught." The Danville papers went further: the Times, quoted in the Richmond Daily Times on July 2, wrote that it was "expecting and hoping to hear of his being lynched." The Register, reprinted in the Durham Recorder, said the rope that ended his life "will not cost the state anything" and printed his description for searchers.
The December item in the Alexandria Gazette reported his arrest and the sheriff's precaution against lynchers without comment.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Jed Pritchett
bases: The papers reported a manhunt by armed neighbors and officers for a Black man accused of assaulting a white child, with repeated statements that he would be lynched when caught (A2, A4, A5), and a sheriff moving him from jail for fear of lynchers after his arrest (A7); no lynching took place in the coverage.

A number of men searched for Pritchett and papers predicted he would be lynched (A2, A5), but no report shows him killed; he was arrested and moved to Lynchburg jail to forestall an attack (A7). The episode is a threatened lynching.

The accusation, escape and search are reported independently by a Danville telegram (A1), the Danville Times (A4) and the Danville Register (A5), and the arrest and transfer appear in a later Virginia News item (A7).

accounts.gist: The child named Pritchett as her attacker; he fled, and men and officers searched the country for him with the expectation that he would be lynched when caught.

accounts.label: Later Virginia News report
accounts.gist: Pritchett was arrested near Durham, N.C., in December, jailed at Chatham, and moved to Lynchburg because the sheriff feared lynchers.

framing.detail: The Danville papers and the Dispatch telegram treated a lynching as deserved and expected: 'he will meet with the fate he deserves', 'hoping to hear of his being lynched', and the rope 'will not cost the state anything'.
The December Alexandria Gazette item reported the arrest and the sheriff's precaution against lynchers without comment.
